response.translation: [343] GALEN: WHOM ONE MUST PURGE, WITH WHAT CATHARTICS, AND WHEN. It is a laborious matter to purge those who have their bodies in a healthy state; for they become dizzy and suffer gripings, the purgation proceeds with difficulty in them, and besides this they also quickly become faint. All these things happen because the cathartic drug strives to draw its proper humour, and, through lacking it, colliquates the blood and the flesh, so that it may draw from them what is proper to it.

We at any rate, by such evacuation, have for many years now prevented both podagra and arthritis that was beginning, and had not yet produced concretions (pōroi) about the joints, from developing. In the same way we have, through the aforementioned evacuation, put a stop in many people to apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy and other such chronic affections. For some, then, it is beneficial that the phlegmatic humours be evacuated, for some the bitter-bilious, for some the melancholic, and for some the serous residue, according to the substance of the affections that customarily befall them. For example, a certain man is seized by melancholy every year unless he is purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn. response.translation: The matter [347] of rest, then, is clear. For as exercises naturally dry, so rest, which is quiet and absence of exercise, naturally preserves the moistures. Food, however, does not moisten simply by being more abundant; that food moistens which is without a strong quality, that is, neither astringent nor acrid nor salty nor bitter. We have sometimes given radishes in oxymel, having fixed shoots of white hellebore into them for a whole day and night, and such a purging from hellebore would be a weak one. Those who have the thorax narrow and for this reason also compressed are the most unsuitable of all for purgations by means of emetic drugs, both the others and above all those by means of white hellebore. For in them some one of the vessels in the respiratory organs ruptures. One must also evacuate the bitter-bilious humour upwards and the phlegm downwards. There are times, however, when it is the reverse, if a phlegmatic humour has collected in the stomach and a bitter-bilious one in the intestines. The melancholic humour, however, must always be evacuated downwards.

raw_text: {"translation": "It is written in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates concerning the seasons: 'In summer purge [348] the upper cavities, in winter the lower.' Moreover, habit is no small factor in the indication for evacuation. For those accustomed to vomiting bear purgations through the upper belly with less distress, whereas the unaccustomed do so not without danger, and more so with hellebore. One ought also to consider the form of the disease. For in phlegmatic dropsy there is need of a drug that draws off phlegm, first through the lower belly, then by vomiting, then by apophlegmatisms. For since what is in excess is spread through the whole body, we shall employ all the evacuations. In ascitic dropsy we shall give one of the water-drawing drugs, just as in jaundiced patients one of the bile-drawing drugs. response.translation: From the paroxysms, too, you will have a guiding mark for the indication of the mode of evacuation, making the evacuations from the upper parts during the paroxysms, and from the [350] lower parts during the so-called remissions. For this is also how spontaneous evacuations bring benefit: during the paroxysms many people vomit and bleed from the nostrils, while in the remissions urine and alvine discharges are excreted. One must above all be on guard about the time of the paroxysmal and critical days whenever you undertake to purge copiously downwards. For when the inclination of the humours has turned upwards, the power of the purging drug will be impeded. In those who are already ill, in chronic diseases one must always await concoction, but in acute ones, when [the matter] is turgid, it is possible to administer drugs at the outset; and this very thing must be done with much caution and circumspection. For there is no small danger in purging badly in an acute disease, because all purging drugs are hot in their powers, whereas fever, insofar as it is fever, according to its own definition requires not only not drying and heating things, but even their most contrary ones, the moistening and cooling. Therefore purgation is not employed by us even for the sake of the fiery heat itself.

raw_text: {"translation": "For we know that this heat, so far as it itself is concerned, [351] is harmed by it; rather, purgation is employed for the sake of the humours that produce it. The benefit arising from the evacuation of the troublesome humours must therefore be greater than the harm which the body necessarily suffers from cathartic drugs. And the benefit is greater if the harmful humour is evacuated both without distress and in its entirety. For this to happen, one must first consider carefully whether the patient is in a suitable condition for such a purgation. For those who come from many indigestions, or from viscous or thick foods, and likewise those whose hypochondria are tense and inflated, or are excessively hot and fiery, or who have some inflammation of the viscera there: all these are unsuited to purgations. These conditions must therefore be absent, and the patient's humours must be as free-flowing as possible, that is, thin and having little share of any viscosity, and the passages through which the purgation is to take place must be opened up. The benefit arising from the evacuation of the troublesome humours must therefore be greater than the harm which the body necessarily suffers from cathartic drugs. response.translation: But in acute diseases, right at the outset, that is, on the first day or not later than the second, when we intend to employ [352] purgations because the humours are turgid, such preparation cannot take place. The exception is if one should perhaps have the opportunity to give unmixed honey-water to be made, with some hyssop or thyme or origanum or goat's origanum or pennyroyal boiled in it, or some other of the things that attenuate in this way. So it is reasonable that in acute diseases we shall seldom have need of drugs at the outset. For the offending humours are not often turgid at the beginning, nor, even if this is the case, would the patient be suited to purgation; indeed he does not even afford us a suitable opportunity to prepare him. The humours are said to be turgid when, having come into more violent motion and flowing over from part to part, they trouble the person at the beginning of the disease, causing pain, causing nausea, gurgling, and not allowing him to keep at rest. Such humours, then, it is proper to evacuate, that is, those in motion, transport and flux. But those already fixed in some one part one must neither stir with any other remedy nor purge with drugs before they have been concocted. For at that time we shall also have nature assisting the evacuation.

But when nature is moved perfectly, there is no need of purging with drugs; when it acts more moderately and more weakly, we ourselves must supply what is lacking by administering drugs, so that the evacuation of the troublesome humour may come about from both, nature thrusting it away and the drug drawing it. But along its passage the gullet (stomachos), and as much of the stomach as lies high up, take up not only the quality of the purging agent but also its substance, which settles in the passage, and they are greatly harmed. response.translation: And it is necessary [356] that the cathartics that are mixed be of like kind with one another and in no respect at variance. Their discord arises not when the one, say, evacuates bile and the other phlegm (for both can be evacuated in the same manner), but when the one naturally sets the purgation in motion at once, and the other long after its administration. For in this way the evacuation becomes irregular, when they are administered together. I call it irregular when, while it already seems to be ceasing, the beginning of another evacuation occurs again.
